Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our observations underscore the need for a comprehensive explanation of cosmic ray anisotropies across the entire energy spectrum. Given the limited understanding of high-energy cosmic sources and magnetic field dynamics, we highlight the anisotropy of the most energetic cosmic rays as a potential window into extreme relativistic magnetohydrodynamic processes, likely inherent in the extragalactic environment itself. Our study reinforces the implication that extremely energetic cosmic rays are likely of extragalactic origin, and highlights the significance of further investigation into the interplay between cosmic sources and the medium through which cosmic rays traverse. Our discovery also points to possible limitations of some extreme astrophysical scenarios proposed to explain ultra-high energy cosmic phenomena. Ultimately, the anisotropy of the most energetic cosmic rays presents a challenging and fascinating puzzle that demands further empirical and theoretical exploration. Our current understanding remains an initial guess, and we anticipate that the definitive explanation for these patterns will emerge from a combination of enhanced cosmic ray detection capabilities and improved theoretical models. Our investigation is accompanied by two supplementary studies, one examining the anisotropy of a more narrow energy range, and the other exploring the compatibility of extragalactic cosmic source models with energy-dependent anisotropy patterns. Both of these companion studies are part of the same research effort that gave rise to this primary investigation, and share a common dataset and methodological framework. Although published separately, they are closely related to the current study, and together the three studies form a unified body of work. We conclude by highlighting the widespread impact of cosmic ray anisotropy research, reaching beyond an understanding of these phenomena themselves

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Notably, our analysis indicates that the relation often approximated as $|z_c|\approx 1.445 R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ is not accurate even for $N=4$. Additionally, we have confirmed that the relation $|z_c|\approx 2R_\chi$ commonly applied for $N=2$ introduces significant errors. Our updated findings are consistent with previous results obtained using the 2-d O(N) $\phi^4$ model. In relation to QCD, our findings imply that the Yang-Lee edge singularity is more sensitive to changes in $R_\chi$ than previously thought. Consequently, our analysis suggests that the criteria often used to define the regime relevant to pure QCD may defined more precisely. Moreover, our investigation indicates that the relevant regime is more narrowly confined than previously believed. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the significance of thoroughly testing relevant universality classes before concluding the presence of Yang-Lee edge singularities. Our research demonstrates the advantages of next-to-leading order renormalization group methods, particularly using the $\epsilon$-expansion scheme, and encourages a reassessment of existing data relating to the Yang-Lee edge singularity in QCD. Finally, our results highlight the importance of distinguishing between Yang-Lee edge singularities and other critical phenomena encountered in physical systems. Our findings provide a basis for revising the value of $|z_c|$ used in analyzing QCD's relevant universality classes and encourage further investigation into the dynamics of field theories in three dimensions using next-to-leading order renormalization group methods. Our research has implications for our understanding of hadron mass scales and the convergence of perturbative expansions in QCD. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Our extensive, high-speed visualization data also reveal the critical role of cavitation in the partial-seal stage. Furthermore, our data indicate that the relationship between the radius of the sphere and the time it takes for the splash dome to close is not directly proportional, with larger spheres exhibiting a relatively longer pinch-off time due to increased drag and greater pressure inside the cavity. Moreover, our research reveals that the relationship between the speed of the sphere and the pinch-off time is not directly proportional in the middle speed range, yet returns to a direct proportionality in the high-speed range, indicating that the pinch-off time becomes largely independent of the pressure inside the cavity at high speeds. Our most intriguing finding is the water-entry interaction into the cavity forming inside the sphere, a process we call the "ripling mechanism", and which we believe is a novel fluid dynamics phenomenon. Our extensive numerical simulations, using a coupled level-set/Volume Autonomy Grid Element Method, fail to fully replicate the results of our experiments, particularly the formation of the rippling mechanism. Nonetheless, these simulations successfully capture the surface-seal regime's early stages, and provide valuable insights into the water-entry interactions at the cavity surfaces. Our studies also highlight the advantages and limitations of various water-entry interaction models currently in use. Our experiments and numerical simulations demonstrate a strong agreement in this regard. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. Our dataset is accessible upon request. Our model's limitations include difficulty differentiating between the wall and luminal contents and the need for further refinement to accurately identify small tumors. Our future plans include exploring other attention mechanisms, integrating multimodal information, and enhancing the model to better handle small tumors. Our code and dataset are available online at the specified link. Our study contributes to the field of medical imaging by showcasing the feasibility and precision of a streamlined clinical approach using solely CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. To facilitate this approach, we designed a unique model based on attention mechanisms and dense blocks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For example, we could utilize description recurrence across different systems or even the same system with different parameters, to serve as a more appropiate comparison baseline. Furthermore, I suggest exploring the utility of description quality improvement as a task in itself, possibly benefiting from techniques used in cross-entropy label noise. Despite the difficulties posed by label variability, it may offer insights into the generation process and enhance the plausibility of descriptions. If we are to utilize the existing datasets, I propose a modification of the WSR (Widely-Used Sampling Ratio) method that takes into account the differing sampling ratios of different descriptions. This approach, which is known to perform well in tasks such as text classification, may provide a more precise description of the target distribution and thus enhance performance evaluation. If we consider the accessibility of descriptions themselves, I propose the use of simple, universally applicable metrics like description length, which could be useful for generating more efficient descriptions. If we consider the alignment between descriptions and the user's experience, I suggest utilizing reference data from user feedback or recurring description analysis across different users and descriptions. This approach will likely require the integration of multiple models and datasets to create a unified framework, which could be challenging due to the differences in data sources and distributions. However, if we consider the current state of the art, which is limited by existing datasets, I believe we have reason to be optimistic about achieving this goal. For example, the development of multilingual models and the availability of multilingual reference data may not be too far-off. This framework also offers an intuitive web-based interface to facilitate the development of the framework itself. Notably, the proposed framework is designed with an open mindset that is not tied to the current techniques and datasets, so it is versatile and future-proof. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In areas where people are more likely to prioritize tradition over changing values, there is a greater demand for misinformation. These findings suggest that the spread of online misinformation is influenced by distant, stable factors that affect the content's acceptability in local communities. As a result, we anticipate that the effects of "The Big Sort" on online misinformation will persist long after the original study, given the ongoing geographic fragmentation of Americans. We also propose potential areas for future research on this topic. We further investigate the circulation of news, distinguishing between high-ceremony forms of misinformation, such as anti-vaccination news, and low-ceremony forms, such as political misinformation, and find that these forms are spread through different mechanisms. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for combating the spread of online misinformation and suggest strategies tailored to local community characteristics. We also provide publicly accessible data and analytical code for replication and future research purposes. We further find that the effects of "The Big Sort" on online misinformation dissemination are stable over time and across different social media platforms. We also find that Reddit comment circulation underestimates the true spread of online misinformation due to the presence of quieter users who do not comment on the content. We also explore the limitations of our study and propose potential areas for future research on this topic. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring ways to incorporate speech patterns into learning algorithms and robot control systems. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we propose a method for comparing the meaning of utterances and present an approach to extend existing testing frameworks for user interaction. Finally, we outline our future research directions and invite participation in this area from the larger community. This research is an extension of our previous work presented at the 2023 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, our further analysis reveals the practical applicability and feasibility of MSDCR in real-world settings. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChengLiUIBE/MSDCR.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating robust, robust quality control pipelines into automated analysis workflows, but also stress the importance of reviewing model generalizability on target populations before deploying them in production. This knowledge is crucial for ensuring that automated quality control systems successfully navigate complex, real-world scenarios involving widespread application of MRI data. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our data show that the electronic and magnetic properties remain stable within the studied Cm content ranges, ensuring the generalizability of our findings. Finally, we predict the interplanar distances in the recursive AuCu3 structure, and our method can be utilized to assess sublattice specific properties in other compound structures. Overall, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts the following physical phenomena: deep inelastic scattering at very low depths, heavy quark formation in proton-proton and deep inelastic scattering, and potential anomalies in neutrino proton scattering. The bilepton model can be tested through experimentation with next-generation particle accelerators and direct observation of predicted composite particles. If supported by further research, the bilepton model could provide a comprehensive explanation for physical phenomena observed in deep inelastic scattering and the solar neutrino problem. The paper also presents mathematical evidence supporting the validity of the bilepton model. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Ultimately, our investigation reveals that the standard ordered generating sequences comprise a free submonoid within the Coxeter group Bn, characterized by its Coxeter presentation and properties related to Coxeter length and the descent set. Our research also involves an in-depth examination of ordered generating sequences for the finite Coxeter group An, which serves as a natural extension to the existing knowledge about the subject. Futhermore, we delve into the relationship between ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set for An. Alongside this, we establish that the standard ordered generating sequences form a free submonoid within An as well. Our most notable discovery in this portion of the study is that the Coxeter length of a state, which can be determined from an ordered generating sequence, exhibits a direct correlation with the number of partial exchanges required to transform the state into the identity state. Ultimately, our empirical observation suggests that the Coxeter length of a randomly generated state in the group An follows a linear distribution. Our research on the finite classical Coxeter group An is largely based on an analytical examination of its underlying dynamics, specifically focusing on the random phenomenon associated with partial exchanges of state elements. Our study offers a meaningful expansion on the existing knowledge about the subject, building upon the foundational work established by other notable researchers. Our research methodology involves a statistical analysis of the Coxeter length of randomly generated states within the group An, which can be achieved through various means, as well as an exhaustive examination of the related dynamics through the partial exchanges of state elements, all set within the framework of the finite classical Coxeter group An. Our study reveals a intriguing connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, the descent set, and the partial exchanges of state elements, which together comprise a cohesive and comprehensive understanding of the finite classical Coxeter group An

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Utilizing this correction, we reanalyzed the Hubble diagram for Type Ia supernovae at $z=7.018$ using the most distant supernova, SN C109, and found that the cosmological parameter inference would remain largely unaffected by lensing, with an error of less than $2\%$ in $H_0$. However, for SN C109, the adjustment to the distance estimate is more significant, with an added scatter of $0.13$ magnitudes and could lead to an increased margin of error in $H_0$ of about $5\%$. Nonetheless, combining this data with the remaining SN Ia sample at high redshift would likely result in a more consistent and precise estimation of the cosmological parameters. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, this demonstration shows that T centers in SOI silicon could provide a straightforward path to implementing quantum communication systems that combine both photon-spin interactions and electronic and nuclear spin control, without the need for additional enrichment of wafer materials. Further research is needed to improve the spin-dependent optical transitions and reduce spectral diffusion. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we propose an intuitive criterion to measure the likelihood of successful desensitization, which is shown to influence the transplants' outcomes. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the importance of establishing compatible transplants, yet with the current scarcity of donors, considering incompatible transplants may be necessary in the future. With this in mind, our goal is to provide decision-making tools for physicians and patients to make informed decisions about transplants. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the word2vec model, highlighting the limitations of these learning algorithms, which can obscure the true underlying structures of the data, especially in sensitive applications requiring careful consideration of corpus properties. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research and its findings are relevant to the class of games involving multiple players. It is worth noting that finding rationalizable equilibria in multiplayer games is essentially the same problem as determining the presence of a rationalizable action profile, which is a more general concept, although both are distinct from learning equilibria. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a versatile tool called `pdf4lhc` that can collectively incorporate a broad scope of PDF candidates, with support for major sets of strong and electroweak PDFs, as well as hypothetical alternative scenarios. The tool enables the automatic application of DGLAP evolution to a substantial list of candidates, including popular choices like NNPDF, ABPDF, and dPDF, as well as lesser-known options like H1PDF and ZEUSPDF. Moreover, it provides the desired PDF sets at multiple QCD scales through reverse interpolation, in addition to offering a range of phenomenological predictions for relevant hard scattering processes. Ultimately, we present `pdf4lhc` as a comprehensive framework with wide-ranging applications in PDF fitting, phenomenological research, and the generation of realistic PDF inputs for various new physics models. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has helped in identifying novel genes associated with microRNA processing, mapping precise mutations associated with a bowel infection and in identifying long-range interaction between a gene and a specific locus. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of recurrence times also aligns with a power-law distribution, where more rare binaries with longer recurrence times exist, and many of these are likely the source of the high energy radiation observed by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The implication is that the vast majority of the proposed black hole population in the Milky Way's center may simply be misinterpreted binaries with extremely long recurrence times. The research also offers a theory for the limited long-term monitoring of radio quiet LMXBs and suggests that wide-field optical and radio observations are necessary to reveal the true population of these binaries. The study's findings are further supported by the detection of V4641 Lyrae, a known LMXB that remained undetected during a previous survey, only after examining recurring X-ray sources with longer recurrence times. The investigation reveals that V4641 Lyrae's total outburst history spans over 30 years and consists of over twenty recorded events, further demonstrating the necessity of extensive monitoring for the detection of these binaries. The proposed explanation for the supposed black hole population in the Milky Way's center also offers a potential solution to the observed population of radioactive binaries known as Type Ia supernova progenitors, which on their own are unlikely and therefore may simply be late-stage binary neutron stars. The conclusion is that many alleged black holes in the Milky Way's center and the bulge may actually be wrongfully classified neutron star binaries with long outburst recurrence times. The research suggests that the correct classification of these variables is crucial as it may lead to a deeper understanding of the late stages of neutron star evolution, possibly through the detection of late-stage binary neutron star mergers that produce massive hydrogen envelopes. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. This paper will present our approach to optimizing bipedal robot walking assisted by thrusters using a closed-loop feedback system. By assuming that supervisory controllers are properly set, we will concentrate on refining joint trajectories to meet specific performance requirements. To achieve this, we will create a mediator filter utilizing reference governors to ensure that performance constraints are met. Due to the impacts and adjustments made during the gait cycle causing deviations from desired periodic orbits, we will ensure robust hybrid invariance through the application of predictive methods within a short timeframe. To maintain hybrid invariance, we will leverage the distinctive features of our model, the thrusters, to our advantage. The key benefit of our approach is that unlike other optimization-based nonlinear control methods, performance-related constraints are met during the single-support phase without reliance on costly numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed thruster-assisted gait control framework allows for the utilization of performance and robustness-enhancing capabilities during particular phases of the gait cycle, a previously unreported aspect. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. In addition, the authors established that the ring of integers from an arithmetic field cannot be found within the set of algebraic integers from a specific field of complex-valued algebraic numbers, which has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. The initial proof for this prime distribution consequence relied directly on Gauss's proof that the total residue map is non-computable. The existing proof of non-computability of the total residue map is now considered outdated due to the simpler proof developed by Wadsworth in 1981. Nonetheless, the results related to the total residue map were not part of Wadsworth's conclusions. The current research extends beyond the findings from the initial paper by Becker-Denef-Lipschitz, demonstrating that the associated Frobenius automorphism, the total residue map, and the absolute value function each have a specific property that prevents them from being computationally decided within certain complex-valued field settings. The current research aims to extend the applications of these results beyond the context of arithmetic fields. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, threshold values are established to determine when the removal of an individual node leads to the main component breaking into two or more distinct components. Additionally, the average size of the removed component is calculated and analyzed in depth. Interestingly, this analysis reveals that an abrupt change can occur, where the average component size increases dramatically as the threshold is crossed. This behavior is analogous to the bimodal distribution observed in random triangle-free graphs, but unlike the latter case, the cause here can be attributed to the network structure itself, without the need for additional parameters. Moreover, this paper also explores and compares different node removal sizes associated with distinct start nodes. By examining Cayley tree networks with variable edge probabilities, the effects of these variations on node removal sizes are quantified and analyzed. The results provide insights into network vulnerability patterns that can be useful for applying and generalizing the micro-level attack model to other network types. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this gate design yields minimal loss of frequency robustness as the number of ions increases, making it a suitable option for practical quantum computers. Additionally, this design exhibits an entropy growth rate that is roughly half of the total entropy generations from both quadratic drifts in laser frequency and ion motion, demonstrating its versatility in practical applications. Furthermore, implementing this gate design on a variety of qubit truncation methods is demonstrated, including a novel approach that incorporates frequency robustness into the entropy growth rate calculations, and the accompanying code provides straightforward tools for exploring these scenarios numerically. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach provides actionable alignment guidance that can be utilized for subsequent processing tasks, such as modeling mouth activity or identifying facial attributes. Our SADRNet code is available on GitHub at the address mentioned in the paper details.

We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. Our data further suggest that the LISA gap occurs due to the interference between cosmological perturbations and the inflaton field, with the relative shift ranging from $2.3\times 10^{-5}$ to $9.0\times 10^{-5}$. The found $\sigma$ and $\beta$ values fall within the parameters of previously proposed models featuring the formation of PBHs, with different mass ranges and formation mechanisms. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. This investigation seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately capturing vote tabulation data, as the system is designed with an advanced spell-checking feature to correct common errors associated with traditional OCR technology, which the research reveals results in iOCR outperforming traditional OCR methods. Nevertheless, the study discovers that even iOCR is susceptible to misinterpretation of specific tabulation layout characteristics, such as the aggregation of individual tabulations and the designation of total tabulations, due to a lack of underlying contextual understanding. Two distinct approaches to address this limitation are tested: a rule-based method based on the creation of if-then statements, which the authors dub the "Smart Fix" method, and a machine learning-based approach known as the "Corrector" model. In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. The proposed estimator and associated theory can be applied to a broader range of linear models featuring dependent data samples. The current research framework extends beyond the mentioned parameters to other settings characterized by dependent data samples, such as nonlinear models, time series models, and genetic data. The study provides a foundational framework for future research extensions, such as learning curves, regularization techniques, and cross-validation methods. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent challenges in addressing this issue, we propose alternative incentives such as tailored risk preferences or storage-specific risk management frameworks. These proposals aim to encourage storage units to optimize their scheduling for long-term benefits, ensuring they behave robustly in changing electricity markets. Given the practical limitations of these proposals, we also simulate different risk management strategies for storage units and analyze their impact on their profitability and robustness in the face of changing electricity market conditions. Our results indicate that appropriate risk management practices can reduce storage units' risk aversion and enhance their self-scheduling performance. Consequently, we advise policymakers to explore and evaluate tailored risk management incentives for storage units to ensure they function effectively in future power grids. Given the complexity of optimizing risk in large-scale power grids, we also propose a new risk assessment approach that leverages recent advances in risk management theory and machine learning models. This new assessment captures the dynamic nature of risk in power grids and provides actionable feedback for optimizing risk in grid operations. Our research demonstrates the value of considering risk aversion in energy storage units through the evaluation of our proposed approaches using real-world data and simulations of real-power grids. Given the widespread adoption of energy storage globally, our research offers practical policy recommendations and innovative methods for managing risk in power grids with widespread energy storage deployment. Given the expected significant increase in energy storage capacity, our research is timely and provides valuable insights for policymakers, grid operators, and the electricity industry at large. Our proposed risk management approaches and assessment methods also contribute to the development of future smart grids with efficient risk management strategies. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples.

In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of dynamic TDD scheduling in challenging cellular environments.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed system demonstrates comparable performance to models trained on larger datasets, as seen in comparisons with current robust machine learning methods. We have made the code and models available for public use.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. In the process, we establish that the standard volume construction satisfies the volume conjecture. The proof involves employing a trigonometric relation associated with $J_n^T$, along with an analysis of the quantum asymptotic property. The research underpins the volume conjecture as arising from the quantum asymptotic property of the colored Jones polynomial within the torus. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, the study validates the integrity of developed models using a natural language inference task, and provides a viable code framework for future WSD research involving semantic understanding and leverage of lexical knowledge.  The study's findings and associated code have been made publicly available to facilitate future development in the field of WSD.  The proposed model has been made available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/zhubiao/bert-wsda. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. In addition to this result, the experiment also established lower bounds on rare top quark decay channels to W pair, W pair with a Higgs boson, and Z pair, at 0.75 nanibarns, 0.85 nanibarns, and 0.45 nanibarns with one nanibarn uncertainty for each, respectively. Furthermore, the distribution of top quark transverse momenta surpassed theoretical predictions from various models, while the central value for the averaged transverse energy of jet combinations exceeded the expected value by an amount equivalent to one standard deviation. The experiment also observed the production of single top quarks in proton-lead data at the same energy, from a 178-inverse-nanobarn data set totaling 8.16 TeV, with a cross-sectional measurement of 3.5 nanibarns and an 8-nanobarn uncertainty. The distribution of single top quark events revealed patterns consistent with expectations from parton distribution functions that incorporate nuclear effects, although the experiment was unable to distinguish between different models of these effects. The duration required to produce a pair of top quarks was found to be 0.79 millisecond with an 0.04 millisecond uncertainty, while the decay lifetime of rare top quarks proved too short to determine with certainty. The experiment also set lower limits on the decay lengths of W pair, W pair with a Higgs boson, and Z pair top quarks at 0.013 millisecond, 0.012 millisecond, and 0.010 millisecond, respectively. The data sets used for these analyses totaled 0.78 picobarns and 0.84 picobarns of luminosity for top quark pairs and single top quarks, respectively. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Additionally, we demonstrated that this approach can be combined with standard numerical solutions to improve the efficiency of such simulations. Ultimately, this stochastic hydrodynamic method provides a versatile and efficient framework for modeling interacting Bose gases in non-equilibrium situations, and its potential applications extend to related problems involving quasi-particles in quantum systems. This approach has been made publicly available as part of the MOLTEN software package. In the course of this research, we also introduced modifications to the harmonic fluid method, addressing an existing issue where the vorticity of the classical fluid field failed to vanish, and presented accurate prescriptions to determine the cut-off rates for correcting quantum fluctuations in the stochastic hydrodynamic model. In the process, we gained insight into the relationships between the various approaches used to model interacting Bose gases, revealing both inherited advantages and limitations, and also identifying the positive-P phase-space formalism as a well-defined but distinct variant of the underlying stochastic hydrodynamic theory. This research was initially published as a series of papers in Physical Review Letters, New Journal of Physics, and Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior results than conventional methods, as measured by model performance and parameter robustness. Our code is available at https://github.com/zuoyuShi/jkfcv. Moreover, our advice to machine learning practitioners considering our proposed approach is to prioritize models that exhibit strong robustness over those with the highest performance, as this characteristic is more likely to ensure successful deployment of their models in real-world settings. In addition, models robust against variance are more likely to succeed in scenarios involving new user input, unlike models overly dependent on their training data, as demonstrated through an illustrative numerical example. In order to facilitate widespread adoption of j-k fold CV, our study visualizes the variance-bias trade-off dynamic through an interactive web-based tool available at https://jikfcv.org/. This enables practitioners to manipulate the underlying parameters, including J and K, as well as observe the resulting impact on model performance and variance in real-time. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Furthermore, we showed that the shape of the absorption profile can be utilized to measure the velocity distribution of ultracold gases, a crucial aspect given the significant influence of initial velocities on distribution shapes in experiments involving free expansion. Our findings are particularly relevant to the study of fundamental physics and the development of precise frequency standards in strontium. For instance, adding recoil effects to accurate simulations of saturation spectroscopy and Ramsey interferometry can enhance the precision of frequency measurements by minimizing systematic errors associated with velocity distributions. Similarly, studying absorption patterns in strontium can aid in developing reliable methods of determining velocity distributions from absorption images, a critical aspect given the limited ability of current techniques to accurately model initial velocities in experiments featuring free expansion. For example, although enantiomeric phase shifts in strontium-III are sensitive to velocity distributions, they cannot be recovered from absorption images due to the failure of current code to incorporate initial velocities correctly, highlighting the necessity of incorporating photon recoil effects and velocity distributions into the optical Bloch equations and related simulations. Our research provides a basis for exploring more complex interactions involving multiple-beam setups, saturation dependencies in various geometric configurations, and the integration of velocity distributions with phase shifts in atomic clocks. Ultimately, our work demonstrates the substantial impact of photon recoil on the behavior of ultracold gases in optical interactions, emphasizing the importance of accurately modeling this behavior in experimental designs and data analysis. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made the paired-permutation test exact without sacrificing its scalability, as demonstrated by our approach being at least 5 times faster than the Monte Carlo method on large datasets consisting of millions of observations. We've also incorporated this exact algorithm into a range of evaluation metrics commonly used in NLP, including the paired-permutation version of the Paillard test. We've made our code publicly available to facilitate the use of our exact algorithm in the community. We've conducted extensive experiments using our paired-permutation test on real datasets consisting of up to 20 million words, and we believe that our results are applicable to a broad range of applications in NLP.
