A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Finally, suggestions are made for potential future research on this data, including an investigation of market integration and the effects of giant ship purchases on industry stability. The methodology used is similar to that employed by Hamilton (2001) in his analysis of gold prices. The shape of the rate frequency distribution is also examined to determine if it supports the idea of a non-symmetric price rule among shipping executives. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a specific kind of veering triangulation, with this characterization being inherently distinct from its definition based on pseudo-Anosov flows. Furthermore, a method for constructing a loom space from a veering triangulation is introduced, and it is proven that this construction results in a loom space topologically equivalent to 3D space. Moreover, it is proven that the volume of a loom space is directly proportional to the volume of its corresponding veering triangulation. Lastly, it is demonstrated that the volume of loom spaces, which are topologically equivalent to 3D space, can be minimized to achieve a value of 1 when their underlying veering triangulation meets specific conditions, with this achievement being an expansion on Pambianco's research. Specifically, it is shown that when a veering triangulation fulfills these criteria, its corresponding loom space's volume can be reduced to 1, with this volume reduction being associated with a specific four-dimensional manifold whose volume is also 1. It is also shown that this four-dimensional manifold is equivalent to a manifold defined by Stefani. It is also shown that for every veering triangulation meeting these criteria, there is a unique four-dimensional manifold with a volume of 1 that is topologically equivalent to this manifold, with this uniqueness being associated with the compact four-dimensional manifold whose universal cover is this manifold. It is also demonstrated that this unique four-dimensional manifold is linked to every pseudo-Anosov flow with a veering return map, with this four-dimensional manifold also being the manifold from which the flow's leaf space is derived. It is also shown that for every veering triangulation meeting these criteria, there is a specific kind of link space that is topologically equivalent to this four-dimensional manifold, with this link space's construction being associated with the volume-minimizing property. It is also shown that this volume-minimizing property is linked to every pseudo-Anosov flow with a veering return map, with this property also being associated with the four-dimensional manifold from which the flow's leaf space is derived. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to estimate the drag experienced by the cylinder in both orientations and how it changed with speed and the fraction of anisotropy. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Moreover, the magnitude of triangular and elliptical flow can be matched by adjusting the initial conditions, allowing for direct comparison and distinction between triangular and elliptical flow components in central collisions. Furthermore, our findings also reveal that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow increases with colliding system size, mirroring the behavior of ratio of corresponding initial condition multiplicities. Ultimately, our results support triangular flow's origins in initial anisotropic geometry rather than quark quadrupole correlations. Our research further suggests that the magnitude of triangular flow in small system collisions is influenced by quark trijunctional flux, in addition to initial anisotropic geometry. Finally, our data also indicate that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow can serve as a potential indicator of quark trijunctional momentum dependence within heavy ion collisions. Our research is relevant to current and future experiments, including the Large Hadron electron collider, and suggests that triangular and elliptical flow measurements are crucial across all colliding system sizes. Our results are consistent with existing findings and have been validated through comparison with leading models, also predicting distinct predictions for star and lead ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider's top energy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Alice-Exp/MPHPT. Our research facilitates deeper understanding of heavy ion collisions' dynamics and encourages further investigation into initial condition generation within particle transport models. Our findings also encourage future research into triangular and elliptical flow within other transport models and molecular dynamics simulations. Our code's transparency aims to accelerate development of new transport models and the creation of more accurate models through model combination. Our results provide a basis for further study into rare quark algebra and initial condition generation within heavy ion collisions. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be viable for both local and global preservation properties, and is evaluated under various scenarios involving both linear and nonlinear systems. Furthermore, the study illustrates the applicability of this method to both conservative and dissipative systems, and provides numerical experiments for both plane wave Allee effect model and the Ginzburg-Landau equation. The results demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness in preserving both global properties and the number of positive solutions, as well as its ability to produce accurate solutions when compared to traditional time-stepping methods. The study also compares the performance of the proposed method with both conservative and dissipative time-stepping methods, and presents numerical data to illustrate the decay/rate of certain properties. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. Furthermore, we present a practical solution for laparoscopic liver surgery navigation by fusing pre- and intraoperative data. This is shown to accurately align with intraoperative blood staining patterns when direct surface data is unavailable. The resulting model-guided segmentation of liver tissue is evaluated using LapSR, an previously proposed method, and reveals a 3.43 times increase in the area of correctly stained regions compared to the intraoperative alone approach. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We hope this dataset and proposed method will facilitate meaningful improvements in estimating self-consistent scene flow. Find the dataset at https://scene-flow-benchmark.github.io/. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouYuan-1998/Adversarial-Metric-Learning. Code and dataset are part of the repository. We encourage interested parties to explore and contribute to the field of self-supervised scene flow estimation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. We present a proposal to utilize a Random Neural Network as a versatile classifying model that combines the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the high classification accuracy achieved by traditional neural networks, showcasing this concept's effectiveness across real-world classification datasets. We also present the design of a spiking neural network based on random neural networks, along with the proposed 'Sleep-Wake' learning algorithm that enables the network to learn from data. This proposal demonstrates the potential of random neural networks as a universal classification model, in addition to providing a readable introduction to spiking neural networks and real-world classification using artificial neural networks. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not a necessary condition for the E2F property by introducing the diamond graph, a non-bipartite cubic graph that only satisfies the E2F condition but not PMH, thus providing an infinite family of such graphs. The diamond graph was first mentioned in a 1980 paper by Schelp, who questioned the existence of an infinite family with this structure. Our work also involves investigating the relationship between the Wiemeler surface and the diamond graph, leading to the conclusion that the surface does not exhibit the properties required by Biggs' conjecture. Our research expands upon various concepts initially explored by other authors. It is noteworthy that the terms papillon graph and diamond graph were previously mentioned in a 1980 paper by Schelp, who enquired about the existence of an infinite family of diamond graphs. Another reference to the diamond graph can be found in a 1986 paper by Wiemeler, who unknown to Schelp, used the diamond graph to create a surface. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, Timeloops system call learning can be an important resource for future secure containerized applications following microservice architecture. The Timeloops project is hosted on https://timeloops.org/.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. Experimental results confirm the advantage of using grid-based representations and the efficacy of the proposed algorithm. Furthermore, target density grids can be made accessible for visualization purposes. A key advantage of this filter variation is its relatively minimal computational demand. The study highlights the tight connection it has with the optimal target density estimation required for sensor management. A practical application of this estimation is also demonstrated. given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our designs offer prospects for achieving 0.5 
Angstrom resolution in a TEM. By modeling the scan of a sample and an image 
formation process, we demonstrate how a programmable phase plate can achieve high-
resolution images on an uncorrected TEM. Our research showcases the versatility 
of programmable phase plates in accommodating diverse TEM setups, with potential 
for applying this technology to other electron optical systems. Our design files 
are available for download, and our research provides a foundation for improving 
programmable phase plates in relation to resolution, current density, and probe 
formation. This development is crucial for advancing electron microscopy through

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our research reveals the individual
migration histories of approximately 500 nuclei spread across the retina. This comprehensive understanding of the
spatial and temporal dynamics of IKNM in the zebrafish retina provides a valuable foundation for exploring the complex
interactions between cell migration, proliferation, and fate determination during neural development. We have also
created a comprehensive, publicly accessible simulator based on our findings, along with the code required to reproduce
our data, images, and results at this link https://github.com/molcylab/retinal_iknm. We hope this research, along with
the associated tools, will facilitate further investigation into the intricate processes underlying neural development.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Additionally, our research reveals the presence of a critical threshold where the overall speed slows down significantly as the number of dimensions increases, and we relate this behavior to the unique characteristics of polar active fluids. Furthermore, our model predicts the occurrence of a unique non-equilibrium phase that resembles the behavior of the discrete Sine-Gordon model. We've also tested our theoretical findings by simulating a model active agent system that follows simple rules and found them to be accurate. Existing literature contains theoretical predictions that match our results, but our research also reveals the limitations of those existing theories. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for understanding the complex dynamics of active fluids in restricted environments and identifies various interesting phenomena that remain to be explored. Our model can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, including the dynamics of active agents within a lattice, near a wall, or surrounded by randomly distributed inclusions. We've also developed a novel method to apply the hydrodynamic theory to active agent systems that maintain polar symmetry. Our research demonstrates that the dynamics of active fluids in restricted environments are influenced significantly by the presence of obstructions, which can be shaped look like disks, spheres, or randomly arranged inclusions, and the resulting patterns and dynamics are highly scalable and dependent on the spatial environment. Our model predicts the occurrence of a unique non-equilibrium phase that resembles the behavior of the discrete Sine-Gordon model, among other phenomena, and offers a useful framework for understanding the complex dynamics of active fluids within confined spaces. Our research also highlights the limitations of existing literature containing theoretical predictions that match our results. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. The research also enabled scientists to calculate the total accretion torque, the strength of surface friction, and the degree of non-spherical mass distribution within these asteroids. Ultimately, studying the rotation of these three asteroids has expanded the existing database of YORP accelerations, which currently consists of six detected cases, all indicating that the YORP effect dominates rotational evolution in small rocky asteroids. Additionally, the success of this study demonstrates the value of observing small asteroids that have active cometary features or show signs of solar wind interaction with their surfaces, as these planets are more likely to exhibit accelerated rotations. Finally, analyzing their spin state can offer valuable insights into the decay rates of surface forces on asteroids with weak gravitational binding energy. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. Finally, the relationship between continuous functions and a related concept called recursive regular languages is examined, including an efficient way to determine if a specific regular language is recursive.

This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've proven the correctness of our algorithm and provide a sample application demonstrating its use in optimizing controller parameters. This optimization problem can be solved using any gradient-based method, but we've found that the Euler scheme performs well. Ultimately, our research focuses on controller design for a nonlinear humanoid robot model, but our methodological contributions are more broadly applicable to other optimal control problems involving variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. We've made our robot simulation software openly available as part of the ``Optimal Controller for Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equations'' repository on GitHub. This package includes the software for calculating the reachable state space and optimizing controller parameters, in addition to the robot simulation tools. Furthermore, we've published an extended version of this research as a technical report. This work is an extension of our previous investigations into finding optimal controllers for a nonlinear humanoid robot model using worst-case performance measures, but it represents a more general approach that could be applied to other dynamic systems and performance metrics. We've compared our controller design with existing approaches using the same benchmark problems and scenarios. Finally, we've made a critical change to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation that enables us to expand the state space that can be reached within a given time frame, thereby extending the efficacy of our controller design method to a wider range of systems. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methods used here provide a framework for investigating the animacy spectrum across different species and in different cultures. The VTC animacy database is available for public use. The study's findings are consistent with a recent theory proposing that the concept of agency underlies the formation of narratives. The research presented in this study forms the basis for examining the neural basis of narrative formation in the brain. The relationship between the animacy spectrum and the formation of narratives has been hypothesized to be interconnected at a cognitive level, yet the underlying neural mechanisms for this relationship remain unknown. The study of VTC's animacy spectrum provides a preliminary understanding of the mechanisms underlying this relationship, while the formation of narratives offers a more complex and higher-level process that represents the result of this relationship. The resulting narrative formation model is called the Agency-Narrative Model (ANM). The ANM was tested using functional magnetic resonance imaging in a new participant group. The results from the ANM are consistent with previous research on the formation of narratives and provide a framework for examining the neural mechanisms of narrative formation in different cultures and across different species. The study of VTC's animacy spectrum and the development of ANM were both tested in the context of Western cultural beliefs about animals but have the potential to be applied in the investigation of non-human primates and in the analysis of cultural animacy beliefs across different societies. The database and the ANM model can be utilized for future magnetic resonance imaging studies of the ventral temporal cortex. The research presented in this study may have implications for the development of effective animal brands in marketing. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how the virus transmitted through that single event continues to spread among community members. This dependence is reflected in a hypothetical example calculating the effective $R_0$ value as twenty-five. The model presented in this report can be applied to a wide range of scenarios involving the transmission of infectious diseases within closed spaces and provides a framework for addressing policy questions related to future super-spreader events. The model's limitations relate to its temporary applicability, as it is designed to describe scenarios lasting no longer than a week. The proposed model assumes that the duration of such events is sufficiently short that the rate of new infections remains roughly constant throughout, which is a valid approximation when comparing the duration of these events to the length of time it takes to recover from a disease caused by SARS-2. The model's name reflects the specific application considered in this report, but its underlying concepts are more broadly applicable to a wide range of transient transmission scenarios. The term "effective $R_0$" value also requires clarification, as it is defined as the total number of secondary infections raised to the power of one, which is derived from the formula $S(e) \propto e^{(R_0-1)/\lambda}$, where $\lambda$ is equivalent to $1/\gamma$ in models featuring a constant infection rate. The term "super-spreader event" is used to describe scenarios with an unusually high transmission rate, which is represented by the variable $\lambda$. The model considered in this report assumes that the variable $\lambda$ varies significantly from the typical value, which is deemed large

As with the currents, this entropy is independent of the topology and isn't continuous. Ultimately, these examples illustrate the value of defining topological entropy for individual group currents F_N. By examining the relationships between the structures of these currents and their underlying groups, we seek to understand the fundamental properties of topological entropy within the context of topological Markov systems

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.  ReCross's simplicity, efficiency, and excellent performance make it a compelling choice for unlocking the full potential of massive language models across various tasks.  Our code is available at https://github.com/leixinyz/ReCross.  Our findings also reveal the critical factors contributing to poor performance in unsupervised cross-task generalization, including the difficulty of selecting relevant existing data, as well as our proposed solutions to address these challenges.  Ultimately, our research demonstrates substantial gains in unsupervised cross-task generalization, with observable improvements in metrics like zero-shot follow-up task performance.  Our approach can be applied to various unsupervised transfer settings, including both single-model and multi-model scenarios, and we showcase the applicability of ReCross in such contexts.  Our research paves the way for further exploration of unsupervised cross-task generalization, while the proposed ReCross method stands out as a concrete solution ready for immediate use. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be accessed in the GitHub repository mentioned in the paper. The paper's contributions are demonstrated by publishing a specific application example that achieves a 23.7% improvement in the private version of the ReLU activation function using CIFAR-10 and a 8.4% improvement in the private VGG16 algorithm using MNIST. The paper further recommends the Bayesian method and evolutionary optimization, and suggests that the choice of algorithm depends on the specific problem being addressed. The paper's findings have implications for the efficient private classification of large datasets and provide a foundation for the development of new algorithms for hyperparameter tuning in DPSGD. The paper's limitations are acknowledged by suggesting the need for further research in the following areas: the development of low-cost, differentially private methods for the evaluation of algorithms and the implementation of robust, secure hyperparameter tuning using artificial neural networks. The paper also offers practical advice for practitioners on the effective application of the methods examined, and provides a general framework that is applicable to other machine learning algorithms and classification problems. The paper further offers a utility-maximizing algorithm that is considered a key contribution to the field, and the code developed is seen as a initial step towards the development of a differentially private tuning platform in the cloud. The paper's aim is to minimize the cost of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, and the most critical factor contributing to this cost is the number of gradient computations required. The paper examines the privacy-sensitive hyperparameter tuning problem from an utility-maximizing perspective, and proposes a novel algorithm that efficiently finds an optimal balance between privacy and performance. The paper further conducts extensive experiments on real datasets, and the results show that the proposed algorithm achieves a 23.7% improvement

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Furthermore, we derive results for the Euler characteristic, namely |\Omega|/N and 1, where \Omega represents the set of pairs (D,\phi) as defined within the text. Additionally, we investigate the homotopy types of these boolean complexes for geometric groups, including Hihn's result that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a point when |S| equals 3 or 4. Lastly, we demonstrate an intriguing connection to the length-minimizing problem of reaching the identity element within W. Our work is an extension of the results by Tenner, building upon her findings published in 2020. Our research also encompasses a broad subset of groups studied by Egorov and Rips in 2003, sharing characteristics with Coxeter groups, allowing an identical analysis. In contrast to Egorov and Rips' random model, our boolean complexes' homotopy types are deterministic objects. We propose that the length-minimizing path to the identity element within W can be visualized as the homotopy type of this boolean complex, also interpreting it as a shellable, simplicial complex of pure dimension |S|-1. We conclude by introducing a new statistic, known as the filigree of a Coxeter group, which is distinct from other established metrics. This new metric, in turn, leads to a deeper understanding of the properties exhibited by filigree groups. Our extensive research is underpinned by a comprehensive theoretical framework along with comprehensive computational results, involving both large-scale simulations and exhaustive analyses of various subgroup settings. Our primary research tools are a combination of both a manual, analytical approach and a more general, theoretical framework. We also developed a complementary, secondary line of inquiry, known as the length-minimizing graph (LMG), which is a more general structure that subsumes the boolean complex structure as a specific instance. We uncover a more general set of properties shared by LMGs, also discovering their homotopy type

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our research provides a quantitative understanding of rumor propagation dynamics and presents a framework for predicting the speed of their spread. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. The advantages of LifeStream are further highlighted by its ability to efficiently handle batch computations, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of scientific and industrial applications. The streamlined version of LifeStream, dubbed \emph{FastStream}, achieves notable performance boosts on benchmark benchmarks, demonstrating the efficacy of its internal architecture. To facilitate widespread adoption, we open-source LifeStream, enabling the scientific community to build upon this framework for future advancements. Moreover, we provide a detailed, publicly-available benchmark suite to facilitate comparison and testing of other stream processing solutions. The performance gains and streamlined versions of LifeStream and FastStream are presented in the accompanying paper code, awaiting further optimization opportunities. The underlying LifeStream engine and related assets are available at https://github.com/yangqa/LifeStream. The FastStream variant can be found at https://github.com/yangqa/FastStream. The comprehensive benchmark suite is accessible at https://github.com/yangqa/streambench. The design of LifeStream and FastStream involves a number of novel stream processing-specific architectural features that yield its performance benefits. These include a novel data layout optimization called \emph{ArrayReorder}, a specially-tailored memory allocator known as \emph{StreamMem}, and a customized scheduler called \emph{FastSchedule}. The performance gains achieved by LifeStream and FastStream result from the effective integration of these features with its underlying engine architecture. The performance advantages of LifeStream and FastStream are extensive, with FastStream delivering a $2.3\times$ performance improvement on a real-world biomedical processing task, and achieving a $1.5\times$ performance increase on the widely-used Numpy library when processing large numerical arrays. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. A practical application of these curves is demonstrated in the context of a particular type of surface in the four-dimensional Euclidean space. The study also examines the relationship between these curves and the geodesics of the four-dimensional Euclidean space. The term Bertrand curve refers to a curve whose associated curve, obtained by connecting the points where the curve intersects a given curve, has curves passing through points where the original curve changes direction at the same rate. This definition holds true in two-dimensional Euclidean space, but it is shown that there are other types of curves in higher dimensional spaces that fit this classification, including the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, which consists of a curve and its associated curve having the same rate of change in the same direction, except when the curve changes direction, in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. The study of these curves reveals that they are part of a larger category of curves that have the same rate of change in the same direction, except when the curve changes direction, in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. A specific type of surface, called the Clifford surface, is examined to determine its relationship with these curves and demonstrates that the curves that make up its axis are timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves. The study also examines the curvature of these curves and determines that they can be classified into three types: constant negative curvature, zero curvature, and constant positive curvature. The paper also presents three examples of timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves: a curve with constant negative curvature, a curve with zero curvature, and a curve with constant positive curvature. The curves with constant negative curvature and constant positive curvature can be found on the Clifford surface, while the curves with zero curvature can be found on a type of surface called the Kundrov surface. The study also examines the relationship between these curves and the geodesics of the four-dimensional Euclidean space and determines that the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves are the result of reflecting the geodesics with respect to a particular plane called the polar plane. The paper also presents three examples of polar timelike (1,3)-Bertrand

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we propose a novel approach called adaptive loss function learning, where the network's performance is steered towards an optimal solution by optimizing loss function with respect to the network itself, rather than a fixed target. We test and validate our approach using real-world image classification datasets, with results showing that it can successfully adapt to diverse classification problems with no additional training required. Moreover, our research demonstrates the therapeutic potential of adaptive loss function learning in enhancing network robustness and reversing neural network 'fingerprinting'. In summary, our discoveries provide empirical evidence to reconsider the conventional loss function landscape, offering a framework for a more flexible and versatile approach that is capable of tailoring the loss function to the specific characteristics of the given dataset, thereby enhancing performance and facilitating network robustness evaluation. We have publicly available code and models to support further research in this area. We have also made our adaptive loss function learning code and models available for use by the community. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. The accuracy of the proposed model is validated through comparison with experimental data from cyclic loading tests. The advantages of this model are demonstrated by comparing it with existing literature models using same test data, showing improved accuracy. The proposed model exhibits higher precision in predicting the mechanical and thermal properties of polymers than existing models. The advantages of this model also extend to lower computational costs required for the same precision levels. The proposed model shows a precise representation of material microstructure evolution during strain-induced crystallization, which remains a crucial aspect for further research. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. A calculation of the free energy of the system is also provided, with the result showing that the free energy difference between the nematic and chiral phases is insensitive to the presence of the London energy associated with the magnetic field, but rather depends solely on the order parameter amplitude. A discussion on the relevance of this analysis to Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also presented in this study. A proposal for an experiment involving the injection of a current into a sample of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also proposed, with the expected result showing that a detection of a change in the free energy of the system could be feasible. A possible explanation for the limited superconducting phase width in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also discussed. A discussion on the relevance of spin-triplet nematic superconductivity in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ to other systems is also presented, with a proposal for an experiment involving the measurement of a magnetic moment associated with a spin-triplet $p$-wave order parameter. A possible extension of this analysis to a calculation of the energy current relation in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also discussed. A discussion on the necessity of considering the influence of the critical current on the magnetic moment in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also presented. A possible explanation for the energy gap anisotropy in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is also discussed

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. The proposed method enhances performance, yielding improved bit error rate at lower signal-to-noise ratios. The highest achievable gain in SNR is approximately 7 dB achieved with a 8PAM CPM. The proposed method can be implemented as a pre-processing stage to further enhance the performance of differential detection over various channels. The optimal delay periods obtained in this research are compared to a 50 ksps experimental setup, resulting in compatible outcomes. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through realistic conditions, paving the way for its usage in various applications. The relevant MATLAB code has been made available with this submission. The code can be found in the supplementary materials of this submission. The relevant code can also be accessed from the following URL: https://circuituniversity.com/wiki/index.php/Differential_detection_CPM. The code is made available under the CC-BY license. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. NISQ-HHL's compact scale makes it suitable for desktop computation. The paper further presents a previously unseen, scalable methodology to calculate the number of qubits and time required for executing HHL on NISQ hardware. The proposed NISQ-HHL framework is open-sourced on GitHub, alongside execution examples utilizing real hardware and simulations of various problems. The research, alongside the associated code, is available on arXiv, on the Quantinuum website, and on the National Institute of Standards and Technology website. The portfolio-optimization application, alongside the NISQ-HHL simulator, are also available on GitHub with associated documentation. The paper and associated materials offer a comprehensive guide to executing the NISQ-HHL framework, thereby enabling the wide spread of fast-quality portfolio optimization across the financial community. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This confirms the effectiveness of the proposed attention mechanism in efficient ASR using multi-modal learning. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In order to facilitate integration with existing research on this topic, we also present results in a format compatible with widely used transmission models, with the aim of contributing to ongoing discussions on the conditions necessary for effective physical distancing in bus transportation. In doing so, we highlight the crucial role that aerosol transport dynamics play in these settings, and emphasize the value of considering the spatial dimension of aerosol distribution when exploring transportation-related public health policies. In addition, we reveal that the widely accepted 'well mixed' model assumes constant aerosol decay rates, whereas we found them to be roughly 1 to 4 times slower, depending on the location within the bus, with consequences for the duration of viral viability and the distance which aerosols can travel. Consequently, our analysis suggests that existing guidelines for bus transportation safety may require revision. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. Additionally, a model based on the elastic scattering hypothesis successfully explains the magnetic anisotropy and Hall effect phenomena observed in the multilayer structure. Moreover, the Anomaltous Hall Resisitivity's sensitivity to elastic scattering could provide a non-destructive way to examine the integrity of thin film layers at the atomic level. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that spin-orbit proximity induction leads to the formation of exotic carriers with skew-scattering properties, potentially enabling the discovery of novel phases in thin film systems. Given the right conditions, these findings may also facilitate the production of advanced materials featuring strong spin-orbit coupling, which could give rise to unusual phases of matter and enable the development of spin-based devices with unique properties. This is especially true for superconductor and semimetallic systems, where the spin-orbit proximity effect may lead to the emergence of novel zero-energy states and the formation of Josephson junctions with unusual zero-bias spectra. This study opens the door for exploring the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in various material combinations and suggests that careful layer construction is as crucial as the material selection itself in predicting future outcomes. This effect can be reversible, allowing for the removal of carrier scattering and potentially enabling the development of materials with diminished defects, where the anomalous Hall effect could persist up to the micrometer scale. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also present empirical data suggesting that many real-world challenges exhibit relatively low prices of serial dictatorship. We further investigate ways to enhance the efficiency of combinatorial optimization solutions by means of a hybrid approach and agent-based dynamic processes. We discover these methods generally result in lower prices of serial dictatorship, although not always with significant improvement. We also analyze the relationship between price of serial dictatorship and various parameters including the maximum achievable value, the price of honesty, and the price of a hybrid approach. However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  The model's reliance on magnetic field strength suggests that more powerful jets found in active galaxies could also be explained by gamma-ray emissions, although this would require re-examining their observed energy bands.  The most compelling guess based on the model's applications is that radio galaxies emitting high energy radiation in the gamma-band have black hole accretion rates that are 10-100 times lower than their most energetic states.  This implies that the true cause of gamma-rays in these galaxies might be related to states of low mass accumulation rather than the galaxies themselves.  The model also led to the prediction that searching for gamma-rays in the energy bands of the most energetic states of these galaxies could be a more productive effort than examining the galaxies themselves.  Finally, the model suggests that the vast majority of hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes goes undetected, meaning that even the central black hole at our galaxy could be emitting a significant amount of gamma-rays in the high energy range, although this would require additional research to confirm.  The model's limitations also became apparent during its applications, highlighting the necessity for a more comprehensive model that considers all electron interactions.  Notably, the model failed to account for the gamma-rays observed in the energy bands of the most energetic states of the galaxies FRII and NGC 4485, suggesting that these regions might be more complicated and requiring alternative explanations, perhaps related to massive star formations. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a framework for a self-adaptive solver that can be used in rivers with stable bathymetry profiles. However, for rivers with altering bathymetry profiles, a new solver is proposed that combines the advantages of PCA-DNN and incorporates the probability distribution of the riverbed profile to adapt to changes in the riverbed, resulting in a better match than the standard form for deep waters. This new solver model, called RBSVE, is successfully tested on the Yukon River. This study is an element of a broader project aiming to develop an autonomous river flow velocity prediction system using machine learning and the shallow water equations, with applications for real-time flood risk management. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. The transformation of the Madsen-Weiss theorem into its equivalent form also involves a straightforward calculation of certain integral coefficients. The initial proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which was a significant achievement in the field of geometric topology, relied on the theory of algebraic geometry. The success of the standard Mumford Conjecture remains a significant outcome of the Madsen-Weiss theorem proof. The proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem was later simplified by Minami. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Given its intricate nature, this problem proves to be a challenging test case to use for developing and comparing different solver methods. Despite the complexity, the research reveals that both BDDC and AMG solvers produce comparable results. Nonetheless, due to the relatively simple implementation of AMG, the advantage of BDDC solutions would only be realized with further optimization of its own algorithm. Moreover, the project's findings are expected to contribute to the development of more efficient solvers for other complex biomedical mechanics problems. Finally, the project's source code is available on a public repository, enabling other researchers to build upon the work done so far. The research received financial support from the National Science Foundation and was conducted in collaboration with the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The project's results will be presented at the SIAM Conference on Computational Science and Engineering in March 2024. The related project on heart muscle simulation has been published in the journal Mathematical Modeling and Numerical Analysis. The project also involves the development of open-source software for solving cardiac mechanics problems, which includes the DOLFIN and FENRIS tools, and contributes to the development of the FEnSuL library. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. The study shows that the distribution of spatial positions can be determined from the corresponding time-dependent variance, thereby providing a universal framework for interpreting time-domain data from fractional Bachelier processes. We also establish that the characterizing parameters of non-stationary diffusion processes form hierarchical structures, which we illustrate using the examples of cubic diffusion and its variant. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for understanding the spread of correlated and varying populations, in addition to considering future research directions. The study's approaches and methods can be viewed as a foundation for exploring non-stationary dynamics within the contexts of animal movement patterns, population dispersal, and microbial cell diffusion. The study's findings have been visually represented through interactive web-based tools that enable users to explore various diffusion processes and their resulting spatial distributions at different time intervals, which can be accessed at the following website: https://diffusionProcesses.shiny.carvena.org/.
