A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The framework is tailored to a specific scenario of counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, with the resulting equation being analogous to the one proposed by Hodnett et al. ["Counterpropagating mode dynamics in loop resonators," Phys. Rev. A 97, 023801 (2018)] but with a distinct derivation. The primary difference between the two derivations lies in the cross-phase modulation parameter estimation. While the initial approach was experimentally validated, the theoretical framework provided here offers a more fundamental understanding of the parameter in question. The developed theory also paves the way for extending the model to include Kerr nonlinearity between different mode types and for investigating the dynamics of optical parametric amplifiers and oscillators. The explicitly general nature of the mode coupling and phase modulation terms makes the theory applicable to a wide variety of optical resonator configurations. The theoretical framework demonstrated in this work can be applied to both classical and quantum optics, and the associated code can be utilized to develop general-purpose tools for optical engineer and researcher. The code utilized in this research is now openly available online, along with the associated research. The framework and code together provide a useful resource, especially for the investigation of quantum parametric amplifiers and oscillators. The theory and associated code are so versatile that they can be applied to a wide range of optical resonator configurations, both classical and quantum. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. As a testament to the framework's flexibility, we have also incorporated L2Explorer into a broader research agenda focused on continuous learning in multi-task scenarios. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. We focus on the application of higher K\"ahler-Einstein metrics to the compactification of the moduli space of pseudoconvex compact manifolds with constant scalar curvature zero. We demonstrate that the moduli space can be extended to include degenerate varieties, and in doing so, we draw on the framework of the Griffiths-Harris-Sato compactification. The discussion also delves into the relationship between these methods of compactification and the fundamental group of the variety. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Additionally, this dynamics likely results from massive galaxies with a significant density bulge at their center undergoing internal secular evolution, strengthened by gravitational waves from massive stellar populations and asymptotic giant branches, and powered by nuclear energy release from the bulge itself. This understanding sheds new light on the internal mechanisms that regulate star formation within massive galaxies. Moreover, it is concluded that while bulge growth does cause the decline of the mass-star formation rate relation, this phenomenon is driven by specific mass density characteristics in galaxy cores rather than simply being a result of overall mass distribution. Hence, the strength of nuclear star clusters, another dense population with low specific star formation rates, also contributes to this decline, suggesting that the relation may be regulated by a minimum threshold of mass density rather than a minimum mass threshold. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates a high degree of transparency, providing insights into the underlying characteristics of X-ray images related to ICU admission and clinical outcomes. From a technical standpoint, the proposed method offers a significant contribution to the field, as it effectively extracts meaningful features from low-dimensional datasets containing lung image data, while minimizing the risk of overfitting. From a practical perspective, the proposed method is considered a practical solution for predicting severe COVID-19 symptoms due to the ease with which X-ray images can be obtained compared to blood sample testing. However, it is essential to note that the proposed approach requires further validation through the use of larger, more diverse datasets containing post-imaging outcome information. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The proposed SABRA model has been openly shared for further research and development. The code can be accessed at this link: https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA-VRD-FPReduction. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. This discovery also raises important implications for understanding the rotational evolution of low-mass stars and suggests that more precise measurements of core and outer layer rotation rates in other giant stars could provide crucial insights for internal angular momentum distribution models. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. The code of the MetaFEND system has been made available open-source on GitHub.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research also reveals that the solution's singularity can be classified into two types, one of which is sharp and the other is generic. Furthermore, the study provides estimates to determine the time of singularity formation and the order of the singularity itself. This research was inspired by the transport equation with fractional decay proposed by Caffarelli, Crandall, and Lien. It has been observed that this type of equation develops a singularity in a finite amount of time, even with smooth initial data. The study aimed to thoroughly examine the impact of the non-local flow and fractional decay on the formation of singularity by extending the original model proposed by Caffarelli, Crandall, and Lien, which only considers the decay of the solution itself. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon. 
Ultimately, the robust exchange interaction in planar silicon can serve a versatile platform for quantum information processing and calculations.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Our research provides a comprehensive framework that integrates graph neural networks and nonlinear dynamics, and we hope it will facilitate future generalization capabilities within this domain. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a further contribution, the GP 2 compiler has been made available for public use through an open-source licence.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Additionally, the framework's versatility in integrated unsupervised and supervised feature extraction is validated through further numerical experiments. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Furthermore, an analysis of model efficiency revealed that dual-path modules and RNN components consistently outperform standard CRNN architectures on various tasks. The corresponding code and model for the DPCRN and EDSR-Based DNC speech separation models have been made available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/zhenghua-wang/DPCRN_EDSR-Based_DNC. Moreover, reproducible implementation guidelines for the DPCRN model have been provided.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. We propose that the shadow radius can be utilized as an observable for understanding phase transition behavior in black holes. If realized, this hypothesis is viable for future observation in experiments such as the X-ray Telescope on the Enhanced Space Telescope. This proposal is based on a theoretical analysis of the relationship between shadow radius, horizon radius, and the multi-phase transition behavior of nonlinear, charged AdS black holes. If shadow radius does indeed reflect the behavior of black holes, it is essential for future research. If not, further understanding of this relationship will require modeling the black hole itself. We demonstrate that the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills framework enables the understanding of non-linear electrodynamics' impact on black hole physics through the shadow radius. This understanding can be expanded to other contexts involving non-linear electrodynamics. We also observe that the shadow radius can arise in other spacetime scenarios, including those with ergospheres from rotating black holes, which may offer alternative, easily accessible mechanisms for understanding the behavior of nonlinear non-Abelian charges. Finally, we propose that investigating the shadow radius in nonlinear, charged AdS black holes will not only enhance the understanding of nonlinear charges but also serve as a bridge between theoretical black hole physics and future X-ray observations. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, we introduce a method to obtain the Wigner function from the optical tomogram by utilizing a Gaussian state as a reference, and this approach is experimentally verified using entangled state reconstruction from an optical tomogram. The resulting Wigner function predictions are compared with those obtained through conventional state reconstruction methods. The generated data serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of various machine learning algorithms designed to accurately predict the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of a quantum state of light. The proposed method offers a valuable alternative for state reconstruction, notably when machine learning approaches fail, and the experimental data is discussed in detail. The research presented involves experimental implementation of the proposal, simulation support, and an analytical assessment of the reconstruction accuracy. The findings provide a framework for evaluating the performance of machine learning algorithms, and the proposed state reconstruction method offers an alternative for failed machine learning applications, particularly in scenarios with large Hilbert space dimensions. The approach has been evaluated in scenarios with and without loss of information, including those involving entangled states, Gaussian states, and states obtained from Malus measurements, and it has been published in the journal Physical Review A. The associated source code can be found in the paper's repository at the address https://github.com/phaeron/WRReverseTomography. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We also present an error-correction performance comparison between PAC codes, polar codes, and conventional convolutional codes. As the CRC length increases, our results show that search-limited PAC codes exhibit decreased decay rates of error-correction performance. We propose an adaptive CRC length allocation policy to address this issue. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of search-limited PAC codes on various scenarios, including a concrete application to a 5.2 GHz WiMAX system. We show that search-limited PAC codes can achieve a 10 dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio required for packet error rate less than 0.01, compared to conventional convolutional codes with CRC length 64. We also present an integrated PAC code and adaptive CRC length allocation design, which can be easily extended to other wireless communication standards. We argue that search-limited PAC codes can serve as a universal coding solution for various low-data-rate scenarios in wireless communication systems. We provide simulation results showing the advantage of search-limited PAC codes with optimal metric function, tight upper bounds on cutoff rate, and the efficacy of the scaling-bias procedure. We are also willing to collaborate with interested colleagues, looking for opportunities to test and evaluate our research with real-world data, and exploring potential application scenarios with system designers and industry professionals. We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space. In addition, we provide an in-depth analysis of how certain biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space are configured in relation to these recurrent operators. Finally, we identify specific examples of biharmonic hypersurfaces, along with an investigation of how their geometric properties evolve over time. This research is an extension of previous findings, where both the recurrent curvature and shape operators were discovered to play a crucial role in biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space, with one of the key contributions being the extension of this property to Jacobi operators. Furthermore, this research paves the way for an extension of this property to Jacobi operators, which is a crucial aspect for understanding the dynamics of these operators, especially in relation to biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space. We have achieved this by conducting an in-depth analysis of how these operators interact with each other and the index of the Jacobi operator. This index will determine the fate of the hypersurface along its geometric evolution. This research was initially presented at the 12th International Conference on Differential Equations in 2021, where it contributed significantly to the understanding of biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space. This research has been thoroughly reviewed and enhanced in order to contribute to the advancement of the biharmonic hypersurface field. A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our research also demonstrates that the recognizable subsets of (Np/q)d include a group that is equivalent to the group of recognizable subsets in (Qd) despite differing from it, and this subset group meets the characteristics of a group known as the monoid of recognizable functions from Q to Q. Our final contribution involves an empirical analysis of regularly expressed subsets of (Np/q)d. Our research builds upon the study presented in our earlier paper titled, 'The Decidability of Semi-Decidable Problems in Base p/q Systems'. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Furthermore, we provide a concise, executable specification of the MongoDB transaction protocols for each deployment, which can be utilized for ongoing work, such as verifying additional consistency guarantees, checking for protocol changes, and facilitating comparative analysis with other database systems. Our effort towards clarifying MongoDB's transaction protocols also facilitates further research, such as validating the consistency guarantees provided by other NoSQL databases. Our executable specifications, along with the checking tools we employed, are now publicly available for other researchers to use. Our study was carried out as part of a larger project that entails evaluating the consistency guarantees of various NoSQL databases, particularly those supporting transactions, and providing streamlined executable specifications for each database, along with efficient checking tools, to facilitate comparative analysis and further research. Our work can be extended to a broader range of NoSQL databases and systems with similar transactional properties. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also observed that the energy flux variations followed the expected pattern of a Rayleigh distribution, with the result of the most skewed distribution being reduced by the closer distance. Additionally, we detected variations in the solar wind habits during the approaches, including different patterns of pressure changes, varying levels of turbulence, and the presence of solar winds with higher energies on the sides away from the Earth, but these behaviors held true across all four approaches. The one variation we saw was that the most extreme distributions of energy flux occurred on the approaches that took place during the solar orbit periods known as perihelion. The result of the symmetric distributions of energy flux near the solar surface could have implications for models seeking to explain the creation of solar winds and the erosion of the solar atmosphere. The reduced variability of the solar winds near the inner edge of the solar system also makes this region more similar to the solar atmosphere found on the outer edge, known as the heliosphere, than it is to the middle regions. The lower levels of turbulence on the sides away from the Earth during the approaches also suggest that the inner edge of the solar system may be influenced by forces that shape the geometry of the solar winds. The data and findings from the Parker Solar Probe missions provide a key piece of information for modeling the evolution of the solar winds during the early stages of the solar system, known as the solar young stage. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness across multiple domains and environments. Nonetheless, certain challenges remain, as the proposed approach requires extensive computational resources and training data. Nonetheless, the proposed technique has the potential to be a groundbreaking solution for speech-emotion recognition in real-world settings. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Despite differences in density and temperature distributions, the fraction of space occupied by the void remains roughly the same. Additionally, the shock wave's thickness also remains nearly invariable at approximately zero for both scenarios. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. The determination of the driving force required for deterministic chaos onboarding is thus demonstrated, offering a straightforward, measurable indicator for detecting it. This research discovers the forced chaos regime present in massive, slow-moving systems, provides a clear physical explanation for the driving force needed for this chaos, and introduces a simple, measurable reference for detecting it. A mathematical model explaining the source of emissions and their connection to stick-slip behavior is also presented. A major processing challenge is tackled by the results, where deterministic chaotic dynamics are confirmed within extremely noisy signals. The methods used can be applied to identifying chaos in other noisy scenarios. The forced chaos regime it reveals is unexpected but present in massive, slow-moving systems, offering a novel perspective on chaos dynamics and its connection to stick-slip behavior that could influence various fields, such as materials science, geophysics, and biology. The outcome also contributes to a better comprehension of chaos onboarding and its driving force, and it paves the way for implementing forced chaos in massive systems and integrating it with their part components. The outcome can be integrated into numerous applications, including the design of continuous discrete hybrid systems, such as mechatronic systems, biological systems, and socio technical systems. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. These measurements were further utilized to adjust beam separation in insertion devices and to optimize beam alignment and filling scheme for future experiments. The results demonstrated the effectiveness and efficiency of emittance scans in providing critical data for LHC experiment operations and future upgrades. The method has been incorporated into the LHC operation procedure and is available for future particle physicists. The presentation also presents future applications of emittance scans in relation to future LHC experiments. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes example use cases, including the simulation of raw data streams for the Simbol-X satellite and the CMB experiments CMB-T2 and CMB-S4, as well as the components of a concept for a future satellite-based CMB experiment. The software is an open source resource available on GitHub, accompanied by a detailed user guide and technical notes on the underlying methodology. The package has further applications in the simulation of raw data for other modern CMB experiments and other submillimetre cosmic observations. The code is designed with modularity in mind, allowing users to easily integrate new models for theoretical forecasts and incorporate the package into existing pipelines for simulated data generation. The package has been tested on high-performance computing environments and desktop platforms, and is compatible with the NumPy and SciPy scientific computing libraries. The package's documentation is structured according to the NumPy style guide, with the code and documentation hosted on GitHub and the paper presented as a pre-print on arXiv. The software and documentation will be maintained and updated in conjunction with the CMB community's future needs and developments. The's4cmb' package can be used to assess the impact of instrumental systematic effects on actual data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, the Cosmic Background Explorer, the Herschel-SPIRE observations of the cosmic microwave background, the Polarisation Sensitivity of the Sunyaev-Zeld'ovich effect in clusters, and the Simbol-X satellite observations of the cosmic microwave background. The package includes an interactive visualisation of the simulated raw data streams for the CMB-T2 and CMB-S4 experiments, as well as the components of a concept for a future satellite-based CMB experiment. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. As for the original word ordering task, our findings indicate that simply using a standard sequence generation approach is insufficient, and we find that manipulating the encoding process of BART, specifically by removing the detachment of contiguous word pieces during training, results in improved performance. Finally, our proposed method, which incorporates the manipulated BART encoder, achieves superior results compared to conventional approaches, as validated by our experiments conducted across two datasets. The code and datasets used in this research are available at https://github.com/XiaoyuTian2018 WORD-OBJECT-Alignment.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The proposed MD-CSDNetwork exhibits a significant reduction in computational requirements while maintaining superior performance, making it a highly efficient and effective deepfake detection solution. In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, it introduces the concept of a certain space distance measure, which it uses to reframe Menger's problems in a more generalized form, capable of being applied to any space with the property of betweenness, thus generalizing its initial purpose within the context of semi-metric spaces. This generalized framework is demonstrated by applying it to specific examples of spaces with the property of betweenness. Lastly, this article concludes by mentioning the possibility of embedding spaces with the property of betweenness into the structure of Euclidean spaces, though it identifies certain limitations to this possibility. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. We also explore connections to the study of number field ramification and the distribution of minima. Furthermore, we discover patterns in the coefficients of the series counting orders with specified minimum ratio properties, revealing connections to the geometry of root systems and the use of modular forms. Additionally, we establish the connection to the characteristic functions of the distribution of the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $1 \in kN_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{Z}_K)$, where $\mathbb{Z}_K$ denotes the ring of integers in $K$. This leads to an examination of the associated inverse problems and results on the number of fields or quadratic extensions with specific minimum ratio properties. We conclude with a discussion on the potential applications and the scope of further research in this area. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our investigation provides a detailed breakdown of the Forsage network over time, showcasing the constant growth of the scheme until its collapse in 2021. Our research on Forsage offers a unique opportunity to examine a pyramid scam through multiple perspectives, including its operational mechanics, user behavior, blockchains, and scamology. This study demonstrates the possible outcomes of combining large-scale scam analysis with underlying technological infrastructure, and highlights the intricate relationship between operators, users, and the guaranteed financial gains enjoyed by the former at the expense of the latter. This research on Forsage also presents an extensive dataset of nearly a million users, along with their geographic locations, earnings, and niche content preferences. This information could be useful for future studies on user behavior, blockchains, scammers' tactics, and economic models. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We estimated a range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the confirmed cluster sample as expected within the galaxy's bulge, determining the ranges for E(B-V) and E/K as being 1.34 to 3.28 and 1.85 to 4.21 respectively, and consequently finding ranges for the distances from Earth and the galaxy's center as being 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs; we also found metal compositions and ages between minus one and four tenths and 8 to 13 billion years; and finally calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band as being between minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. As a result, the limited understanding of this state has been rectified, providing a clearer picture of its intricate nature. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, the paper proves the approach's relationship to multilayer networking and provides the code to replicate results publicly on GitHub. 

This approach can be considered a beginning point for more advanced community detection methods, especially when the requirements of linearization and state similarity need to be balanced carefully. This is achieved by parameterizing the state similarity graph dynamically, which is deemed a promising and accessible way to explore non-linear relationships between communities of a system that changes over time.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the reliability of gradients further contribute to the understanding of this novel approach. The code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/huangcl1998/SparseGAN.

However, if the spread is extensive, the probability of finding it will increase significantly, although this might be confused with the emergence of life independently in different systems. Therefore, the search for interstellar panspermia needs to consider all past and future star formations. If successful, it could lead to a deeper understanding of the origins of life in the universe. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Ultimately, our most preferred model offers the highest precision in estimating population density and provides a suitable framework for future research.  This model demonstrates a precision boost of 43.6% in estimating density and 25.5% in estimating the average encounter distance when using telemetry data for parameter estimation.  Additionally, it offers a convenient framework with a 20.1% precision gain in estimating the average encounter distance when using capture data alone.  We recommend this model for future studies on the integration of capture-recapture and resource selection methods.  This model is particularly valuable for wildlife studies in areas with complex population structures and provides a precision boost of 37.5% in estimating density when using capture data alone.  We propose an algorithm to facilitate the estimation of model parameters via Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations with proposed updates of model parameters and resource selection function parameters.  We also introduce a data augmentation technique to enhance the precision of density estimation by proposing behind-the-scenes density labels for captured animals.  We recommend this model strongly, especially for the study of mobile wildlife populations, due to its precision-gaining advantages in estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. Our approach can be incorporated into various optimization methods, facilitating the discovery of optimal multilayer configurations that yield stable, synchronized states. As a notable application, we demonstrate how to modify our approach to analyze a model of global climate dynamics. This analysis reveals that a synchronized state can be achieved by identifying the most connected nodes and connecting the remaining nodes in a specific distance-based range. As a result, we can deduce the conditions required for a stable synchronized state in the global climate system and map its evolution over time. Finally, our method reveals the optimal multilayer configuration required for synchronization, which we observe applies to other complex systems exhibiting similar dynamics. Our approach has been made available as part of the PyDy Python package, enabling the integration of dynamical system models with multilayer network architectures and facilitating the examination of their dynamics through the joint matrix representation. This representation can be utilized in various optimization methods and has been employed in the integration of nonlinear nonlinear models with nonlinear solutions, demonstrating the versatility of this approach. This approach has implications for the examination of nonlinear nonlinear models featuring nonlinear solutions and may be applied in various optimization methods, including the discovery of optimal multilayer configurations that yield stable, synchronized states. This approach has been incorporated into the PyDy Python package, a comprehensive platform for the examination of dynamical system models with multilayer network architectures. This package enables the integration of nonlinear nonlinear models with nonlinear solutions and provides access to the joint matrix representation, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems and informing the development of efficient optimization methods. This package has been put to use in the analysis of a model of global climate dynamics, a nonlinear nonlinear model featuring nonlinear solutions

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This task is demonstrated through a specific example based on a 3D configuration space. A hypothetical constant $\Lambda$ is also introduced as a measure of scale, but its physical significance is not understood in this context. The term "Einstein operator" is coined, and this work establishes its deep connection to the Einstein field equation, although it is unclear how Einstein arrived at it. The paper also touches on the idea that the Einstein operator can be expressed in terms of the Riemann curvature tensor, but this relation is not used in its current form. Instead, it is shown that both operators are invariant under the same set of symmetries, namely the $O(3,1)$ group, although this fact was unknown until now. The relationship between the Einstein operator and the Riemann curvature tensor is understood only when the 3D configuration space is flat. Ultimately, this work reveals a fundamental limitation of the Einstein operator, specifically that it cannot be parameterized by the Einstein tensor alone, demonstrating the widespread misconception among renowned scientists was not a mistake, but rather an intuitive, though incorrect, generalization. The associated mathematical concepts, including the use of the clue of the vanishing differential rank of the differential module, provides valuable insights into the nature of the Einstein operator, offering an engaging and thought-provoking exploration of its underlying structure. The paper's main conclusions are validated through the analysis of second-order Einstein operators on a 3D configuration space. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once modified, the code can be tested again using this same process until all problems are resolved. Our approach was developed using a set of simple grid-based games as a testing platform, yielding a concise and easily navigable set of rules for each game that can be used for verification and testing purposes. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The design of the algorithm is adaptable to various network types, including those described as 'powerless' and'mobile'. The design of the algorithm has applications in various fields beyond complex network research, including surveying, sociology studies, geography research, urban planning, and internet protocol development. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Moreover, our results show that this method yields the same physical solutions as the default approach, thus providing a supplementary tool for constructing high-quality initial data. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Moreover, we draw implications for the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials by analyzing the underlying physics, and explore potential applications in harvesting waste heat. Our research demonstrates that the anomalous Nernst effect and Hall effect in these materials share a common origin, and that the anomalous Nernst coefficient can be tailored by modifying the material's electronic structure. Ultimately, our study reveals the potential of antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN for high-performance thermoelectric applications, and paves the way for future investigation into the anomalous Nernst effect in other magnetic materials with strong spin-orbit coupling. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The proposed framework also shows potential for use in other self-sensing materials and engineering projects involving critical project safety. 
The current framework requires further improvement, particularly in reducing the computational time required for damage reconstruction, which currently ranges from 20 to 40 minutes. 
The accuracy of the proposed method is evaluated using different defect sizes and shapes, and the importance of using a realistic simulation environment is demonstrated by comparing the results of actual and simulated EIT measurements. 
The proposed method's accuracy is evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE) and the difference in area (DA) between reconstructed and actual damage areas. 
The feasibility of the method is assessed by conducting experiments with various hole sizes and locations on CNF-GFRP composites, as well as with impact-induced delaminations created using a drop weight tester. 
The developed method's effectiveness is demonstrated by comparing the accuracy of damage reconstructions generated through the genetic algorithm-based physical model (GA-PHME) with those produced through the traditional NCT method, which relies on a perfect ellipse to model damage cross-sections. 
The GA-PHME's superiority over NCT is confirmed by the significantly smaller DA values obtained with GA-PHME, which also demonstrates the robustness of the method by accurately detecting damage in cases where the material includes random nanofiller distributions, which can slightly affect the shape of the damage
