Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced and is available online.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN succeeds in modeling complex, hierarchical structures and achieves the lowest distortion score among competing methods. This confirms that learning from hyperbolic geometry alone is sufficient to capture complex graph structures and that LGCN represents a highly efficient and effective network for graph learning. This is further illustrated by analyzing the learned node features and comparing LGCN with other distortions-based methods. This paper is an extended version of the paper presented at IJCAI 2023, and it includes additional research, experimental data, and evaluations. This extends the initial research beyond what was possible in the conference setting. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this method allows us to solve the inverse problem through the use of a regularization technique. The solution to the source term is obtained by combining the discrete operator theoretical approach with the standard Tikhonov regularization. This methodology is efficient and offers a straightforward implementation. Numerical results, obtained using a finite element method, demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of this strategy. variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The harmonic gauge approach also enables the inclusion of external vector and scalar fields, leading to new effects in the linearized massive gravity scenario.  The development of a harmonic gauge approach can be applied to other linearized metric gravity theories, such as the Palatini and self-tuning versions.  The utility of the harmonic gauge formalism is demonstrated by linearizing the massive gravity theories within both the Fierz-Pauli and Palatini frameworks, which were previously found to be difficult.  The method also proves useful for studying the linearized massive gravity theories in contexts involving external sources and those with varying spacetime metrics.  The resulting harmonic gauge equations and the corresponding perturbation equations are found to be well-behaved under the adoption of a particular covariant gauge that is connected to the physical properties of the linearized massive gravity theories. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, the magnetic moment of Ru in RuO$_2$ may require $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing to be fully explained, and such mixing can also impact the calculation of optical spectra and other physical properties. The general methodology we introduce can be applied to other molecular or crystalline systems featuring complex electron configurations. The specific results we present are relevant to materials scientists studying oxides of titanium, vanadium, cobalt, iridium, and osmium. The proposed approach can be incorporated into other methods, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between spin-orbit coupling, electron-electron interactions, and crystal field effects on orbital behavior. The impact of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing on the distribution of electrons within molecular ions or the band structure of solids will then reveal previously unexplained experimental findings and guide theoretical models of novel phases and reaction pathways. The most straightforward applications relate to transition metal compounds with cubic symmetry, where the effects of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing are most pronounced, given the minimal perturbation of the underlying crystal field split levels. The relevance of these findings to experimental observations in RuO$_2$, LiRuO$_2$, NaRuO$_3$, KIrO$_3$, and OsO$_2$ is particularly significant. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for multiple interesting experiments and promising future possibilities. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is particularly suited for
experienced professionals in the field of spatial science, geography, landscape
architecture, and engineering, as well as researchers in social and medical
fields, among others. The guide provides a brief introduction to each method,
along with a step-by-step workflow for implementing it in ViDaExpert. The
associated dataset allows readers to reproduce the examples presented. The
application's functionality is extensively demonstrated through a case study
involving environmental parameters and species data in the Valsesia region of
Italy. The result is a viable, intensive toolkit for executing complex
analyses and presenting results graphically, offering a seamless integration of
statistics, visualization, and interaction within a single, integrated
environment. The application is available for Windows platforms following
registration with the manufacturer. The employed dataset is publicly accessible
on the author's website. The paper was presented at FoSSGeO'04, the first
Workshop on Free Software in Geographical Research, Genova, Italy, September
22--24, 2004. The research was financially supported by the Valsesia Park
Authority and the Province of Vercelli, Italy, within the Valsesia 2000--2002
project, encompassing environmental and biodiversity research in the Valsesia
region, Italy. The associated dataset was provided by the Valsesia Park Authority
and the Province of Vercelli, Italy. The application was developed using Java
and is platform-independent. The source code of ViDaExpert is freely available
on the author's website, under the GNU Public License. The research was
conducting within the Department of Landscape, Plant Environment and Agricultural
Engineering (DiSLA), University of Torino, Italy. The paper was discussed at
